node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - 55% of malpractice cases come from miscommunication between patients and caregivers.md
body:
## Potentially Relevant Papers

### Supporting Evidence

- [[@Hyunjung_2024_Factors_contributing#^Hyunjung-2024-Factor-L6]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > 55.9% explained by proportion of patients with limited English proficiency
  > *The evidence directly validates the claim by showing a nearly identical percentage (55.9%) related to communication barriers, specifically language proficiency, which suggests miscommunication is a primary driver of malpractice cases*
- [[@Svetlana_2023_Diagnostic_error#^Svetlana-2023-Diagno-L5]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > The study analyzed a total of 7,436,737 patients across 20 included studies.
  > *Large sample size of over 7.4 million patients across 20 studies provides robust statistical power to evaluate claims about malpractice case origins, suggesting high credibility for the communication-related malpractice finding*
- [[@Joseph_2017_Information_Mismatch#^Joseph-2017-Informat-L6]] (confidence: 0.85)
  > Five key components contributing to communication ineffectiveness were identified: (1) excessive information volume, (2) complex terminology and conceptually difficult information presentation, (3) patient-perceived irrelevant information, (4) unintentional inhibition of patient engagement and question-asking, and (5) vague discussions of screening and prevention recommendations.
  > *The evidence directly describes specific communication barriers that could lead to patient misunderstandings and potential malpractice claims, systematically explaining how communication breakdowns occur in healthcare settings*
- [[@Cheston_2018_Evaluating_Feasibility#^Cheston-2018-Evaluat-L5]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > The percentage of encounters with LEP patients involving interpreters increased from 0% to 63%.
  > *Increase in interpreter use suggests potential improvement in communication between patients and caregivers, which could directly relate to reducing miscommunication and potentially lowering malpractice risks*
- [[@Jang_2019_Limited_English#^Jang-2019-Limited-En-L7]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > For individuals with LEP, the odds of having communication problems in healthcare settings increased by 4.95 times.
  > *The evidence highlights significant communication problems for patients with limited English proficiency, which suggests communication barriers can substantially increase the risk of medical misunderstandings that could lead to malpractice cases*
- [[@Kornbluth_2022_Communication_methods_1#^Kornbluth-2022-Commu-L5]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > Over 80% of patients with limited-English proficiency spoke English 'not well' or 'not at all'.
  > *Evidence about language barriers suggests communication difficulties could contribute significantly to potential medical misunderstandings, which aligns with the claim about miscommunication causing malpractice cases*
- [[@Mulpur_2021_Reducing_Barriers#^Mulpur-2021-Reducing-L3]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > The hospital increased utilization of language assistance for patients with limited English proficiency by leveraging existing technologies like telephone interpretation with wearable communication devices.
  > *Evidence suggests proactive communication strategies can reduce miscommunication risks, which is directly linked to the claim about communication-related malpractice cases. By improving language access and communication technologies, the hospital likely aims to address communication barriers that contribute to potential medical errors and malpractice risks.*
- [[@Platter_2019_Completeness_Written#^Platter-2019-Complet-L5]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > The mean completeness of language-appropriate discharge guidance for Spanish-speaking families was 16.0% (95% CI 11.5%-20.4%).
  > *Low discharge guidance completeness for Spanish-speaking families suggests significant communication barriers, which could contribute to miscommunication and potential malpractice risks*
- [[@Schenker_2011_Patterns_interpreter#^Schenker-2011-Patter-L12]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > Only 6% of patients reported that nurses spoke their language well.
  > *Poor language communication can significantly impede effective patient-caregiver interactions, which could increase the likelihood of miscommunication and potential malpractice risks. The evidence that only 6% of patients report nurses speaking their language well suggests substantial communication barriers that could contribute to misunderstandings and potential medical errors.*
- [[@Semere_2019_Caregiving_Older#^Semere-2019-Caregivi-L7]] (confidence: 0.80)
  > Only 12% of patients reported having access to professional interpreters at the time discharge instructions were provided.
  > *Low interpreter access suggests communication barriers that could contribute to misunderstandings and potential malpractice, lending credibility to the claim about miscommunication leading to malpractice cases*

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - A Spanish-language adaptation of an HIV mHealth app achieves good usability and acceptability for Latinx PWH while surfacing engagement barriers for iterative design.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Spanish-language HIV mHealth app ConexionesPositivas scored 75 on the System Usability Scale (good usability) - @Kristen_2023_Optimizing_usability]]
- [[EVD - CP users perceived positive impacts of the app on medication-adherence self-monitoring, mood-stress check-ins, and provider communication - @Kristen_2023_Optimizing_usability]]
- [[EVD - CP users identified engagement barriers (privacy, low literacy, lack of personal connection, repetitiveness) and requested more interactivity and personalization - @Kristen_2023_Optimizing_usability]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

This is a usability/user-centered-design claim, not an effectiveness claim. The quantitative SUS score (75, "good") and the predominantly positive perceived-impact and strengths themes establish usability and acceptability for a Spanish-speaking Latinx population of PWH; the barriers and suggestions themes (privacy, low literacy, lack of personal connection, repetitiveness; requests for interactivity and personalization) constitute the actionable engagement findings that the user-centered process was designed to surface. The "positive impact on medication adherence" figures are self-reported perceptions elicited by direct prompting, not measured adherence outcomes; the paper explicitly defers actual outcome measurement to future work.

> "Future research can identify how these changes impact usability and over time, how mHealth participation can enhance engagement in care and clinical outcomes." (Kristen, 2023)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - A medical Spanish curriculum for resident physicians increases language-concordant encounters and reduces reliance on interpreter phones.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Residents trained in a medical Spanish curriculum spoke Spanish with more LEP patients and used translator phones less - @Stoneking_2016_Does_Spanish]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

Training providers as bilingual/dual-role clinicians shifts care toward direct language-concordant communication and away from interpreter-phone use, which the authors describe as slower, lower-quality, and impersonal. This is a single-program, non-randomized comparison, so the claim remains tentative.

> "resident physicians feel that becoming proficient in medical Spanish improves their efficiency in the ED as they save time by not having to use interpreter phones" (Stoneking, 2016)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Bilingual-provider language concordance is associated with greater patient satisfaction and adherence among Spanish-speaking LEP ED patients.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Patients rated visit satisfaction and resident Spanish ability higher for curriculum-trained residents - @Stoneking_2016_Does_Spanish]]
- [[EVD - Among LEP patients who followed medical recommendations after a Spanish-spoken encounter, most were seen by curriculum-trained residents - @Stoneking_2016_Does_Spanish]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

Spanish-speaking LEP patients treated by curriculum-trained (South Campus) residents rated their visit satisfaction higher and, in the small adherence subset, were disproportionately represented among those who followed medical recommendations. The association is in the expected direction but rests on a small, underpowered, non-randomized pilot.

> "Preliminary data suggest that incorporating Spanish language and cultural competency into residency training has an overall beneficial effect on patient satisfaction and adherence to medical recommendations in Spanish-speaking patients with LEP." (Stoneking, 2016)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Certified dual-role nurse interpreters improve the hospital experience of Spanish-speaking LEP patients by brokering communication.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Dual-role nurses observed Spanish-speaking patients show visible relief and ease once an interpreter brokered communication - @L_2023_Dual-role_nurse]]
- [[EVD - Without qualified interpretation Spanish-speaking patients experienced miscommunication confusion and anger during hospital stays - @L_2023_Dual-role_nurse]]
- [[EVD - Concentrating Spanish-speaking patient assignments on dual-role nurses added time-consuming interpreting burden and frustration - @L_2023_Dual-role_nurse]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

By serving as broker between the health care system and the patient, certified dual-role nurse interpreters were perceived to convert a discordant, error-prone, anxiety-inducing encounter into one where patients felt relief, were put at ease, and became active participants in their own care. The evidence is nurse-perceived and qualitative (four participants, one hospital), so the mechanism is plausible and consistently reported but not quantified or generalizable.

> "Of note, all nurse participants perceived they were able to break the language barrier through their dual‐role as nurse and certified medical interpreter." (L, 2023)
>
> "Having certified nurse interpreters deter errors in healthcare and enable patient empowerment through education and advocacy." (L, 2023)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Culturally integrated, language-concordant diabetes nutrition education improves dietary adherence for LEP Chinese American patients and is feasible within usual clinic services.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Dietary adherence (adapted Mediterranean diet score) significantly improved with culturally integrated nutrition counseling but worsened with usual DSME - @Ho_2020_Pilot_Cluster]]
- [[EVD - Culturally integrated nutrition counseling was feasible to deliver within an existing clinic and 100% of intervention participants rated the bilingual booklet as helping their learning - @Ho_2020_Pilot_Cluster]]
- [[EVD - Dietary self-efficacy, weight, and HbA1c trended better with integrative counseling but no clinical or attitudinal outcome reached significance - @Ho_2020_Pilot_Cluster]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

The adherence benefit was demonstrated for one of two food-frequency measures (adapted Mediterranean diet score), and clinical outcomes (weight, HbA1c) did not reach significance in this small pilot. The feasibility argument rests on low added provider burden (a single Chinese-medicine practitioner coteaching) and high acceptability of the bilingual materials.

> "INC shows promise as an integrative health care educational intervention that can be delivered alongside or as part of usual DSME in clinic settings with the additional expertise of a Chinese medicine practitioner." (Ho, 2020)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Hospitalized patients with limited English proficiency receive less numeric pain assessment and fewer opioids than English-speaking patients.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Patients with LEP had the lowest adjusted odds of numeric pain ratings (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.58-0.65) - @Aksharananda_2023_Pain_Assessment]]
- [[EVD - English-speaking patients received substantially more daily opioids (MMEs) than patients with LEP across all pain assessments - @Aksharananda_2023_Pain_Assessment]]
- [[EVD - Patients with LEP had the highest proportion receiving behavioral pain tools, suggesting interpreter underutilization - @Aksharananda_2023_Pain_Assessment]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

Across a large retrospective cohort of general medicine inpatients, language discordance was associated with a documented disparity in both how pain was assessed and how it was treated: patients with LEP had the lowest adjusted odds of receiving a numeric (Numeric Rating Scale) pain assessment and received the fewest daily opioids within every pain-assessment category. The authors interpret the elevated use of behavioral assessment tools for patients with LEP as probable interpreter underutilization, linking the assessment-tool disparity to a plausible mechanism. The association is robust in magnitude and adjusted for major confounders, but it is single-institution and observational, and interpreter-use data were not directly linked to individual assessments.

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Integrating early-warning-score monitoring and interpreters into the rapid response system reduces post-activation mortality for patients with limited english proficiency.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Post-RR activation mortality among LEP patients decreased from 7.42% to 6.09% with special cause variation after the intervention - @Lauren_2024_Quality_Improvement]]
- [[EVD - Process measures, length of stay, and escalation of care showed no special cause variation after the intervention - @Lauren_2024_Quality_Improvement]]
- [[EVD - Disease severity (DI score) at RR activation rose slightly post-intervention with special cause variation - @Lauren_2024_Quality_Improvement]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

A modified rapid response system that paired EHR-dashboard monitoring of early warning scores with systematic interpreter integration was associated with a special-cause decrease in post-RR-activation mortality for LEP inpatients (7.42% → 6.09%). The effect on mortality stands alone: process measures, length of stay, and escalation of care showed no special cause variation (see [[EVD - Process measures, length of stay, and escalation of care showed no special cause variation after the intervention - @Lauren_2024_Quality_Improvement]]), and disease severity at activation actually rose slightly (see [[EVD - Disease severity (DI score) at RR activation rose slightly post-intervention with special cause variation - @Lauren_2024_Quality_Improvement]]). As a single-center pre-post pilot with small death counts, the claim is promising but tentative.

> "In this pilot study, prioritized tracking, utilization of EWS-triggered evaluations, and interpreter integration into the RR system for LEP patients were feasible to implement and showed promise for reducing post-RR system activation mortality." (Raff, 2024, p. 1103)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Interpreting services increase diagnosis accuracy for patients with limited english proficiency.md
body:
## Potentially Relevant Papers


### Contradicting Evidence

- [[@Allar_2022_Lost_translation_1#^Allar-2022-Lost-tran-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Respondents identified systematic exclusion of patients with limited English proficiency (LEP) or significant barriers to implementing patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) for these patients.
  > *The evidence suggests systematic exclusion of patients with limited English proficiency, which implies diagnostic challenges rather than more accurate diagnoses when interpreting is used*
- [[@Altaf_2025_Disparate_Use#^Altaf-2025-Disparate-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > LEP status was associated with a 14% lower likelihood of receiving CT/MRI in the ambulatory setting (OR = 0.86, p < 0.05).
  > *Evidence indicates that limited English proficiency is associated with lower likelihood of receiving diagnostic imaging, which suggests less accurate diagnostic investigation, opposite to the claim that interpreting improves diagnostic accuracy*
- [[@Bauer_2010_Impact_patient#^Bauer-2010-Impact-pa-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Untrained interpreters' errors may have greater clinical impact, potentially compromising diagnostic accuracy and clinicians' detection of disordered thought or delusional content.
  > *Evidence suggests that untrained interpreters can introduce errors that may compromise diagnostic accuracy, which directly challenges the claim that interpreting leads to more accurate diagnoses*
- [[@Betzamel_2023_Longer_Times#^Betzamel-2023-Longer-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Patients who required interpreter use were 2.4 times more likely to experience extended total time to appointment (TTTA) (odds ratio = 2.42, 95% confidence interval = 1.84-3.18, p < .001).
  > *The evidence suggests that interpreter use is associated with longer appointment times, which could potentially indicate less efficient diagnosis processes. Extended total time to appointment might imply more complexity or difficulty in obtaining an accurate diagnosis, contrary to the claim of more accurate diagnoses.*
- [[@Betzamel_2023_Longer_Times_1#^Betzamel-2023-Longer-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Patients who required interpreter use were 2.4 times more likely to experience extended TTTA compared to patients who did not require an interpreter (odds ratio = 2.42, 95% confidence interval = 1.84-3.18, p < .001).
  > *The evidence suggests patients requiring interpreters experienced significantly longer time to treatment/assessment (extended TTTA), which implies potential diagnostic challenges rather than more accurate diagnoses*
- [[@Bischoff_2010_Communicating_foreign#^Bischoff-2010-Commun-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Between 43% and 86% of respondents relied mainly on patients' relatives and bilingual employees for linguistic assistance, depending on the language.
  > *Evidence suggests that healthcare providers often rely on non-professional interpreters (relatives and bilingual employees) rather than professional interpreting services, which likely reduces diagnostic accuracy and undermines the potential for precise medical communication*
- [[@Choe_2021_Disparity_Nurse#^Choe-2021-Disparity--L8]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Nurses were significantly more likely to discuss all safe discharge components in English-proficient (EP) encounters compared to LEP encounters (53% vs 9%; P < .001).
  > *Evidence suggests communication barriers exist without interpretation, showing fewer discharge safety discussions in limited English proficiency (LEP) encounters, which implies less accurate communication and potentially less accurate diagnosis without proper interpreting*
- [[@Clara_2025_Interpreter_Modalities#^Clara-2025-Interpret-L5]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Limited English proficiency patients had higher 72-hour unplanned revisit rates (2.8%) compared to controls (0.7%), which was statistically significant (P = .05).
  > *Higher unplanned revisit rates suggest interpretation may not be improving diagnostic accuracy, as more revisits could indicate initial diagnoses were less precise*
- [[@Debbie_2023_Hidden_Disparities_1#^Debbie-2023-Hidden-D-L5]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Multivariable logistic regression showed significantly lower odds of being provided next steps for Mandarin-speaking callers (OR 0.02, 95% CI 0.01-0.04) compared to English-speaking callers.
  > *The evidence suggests Mandarin-speaking callers were significantly less likely to receive next steps, indicating poorer communication and potentially less accurate diagnoses when interpretation is not effectively implemented*
- [[@Debbie_2023_Hidden_Disparities_1#^Debbie-2023-Hidden-D-L6]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Multivariable logistic regression showed significantly lower odds of being provided next steps for Spanish-speaking callers (OR 0.04, 95% CI 0.02-0.06) compared to English-speaking callers.
  > *The evidence suggests Spanish-speaking callers were significantly less likely to receive next steps compared to English-speaking callers, which implies communication barriers persist even with interpreting services, thus contradicting the claim of more accurate diagnoses*

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Interpreting services reduce recurrence rates for patients with limited english proficiency.md
body:
### Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM). See also the (redundant) grounded claim [[CLM - Professional interpretation at admission or discharge lowers 30-day readmission for LEP inpatients]] — candidate for merge.

- [[EVD - LEP inpatients with no interpreter on admission or discharge had a higher 30-day readmission rate (24.3% vs 14.9%) - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]
- [[EVD - odds of 30-day readmission for the LEP compared with EP group was lower during the intervention period when professional interpreter services via telephone were available, but was roughly equivalent during pre-and post-intervention periods]]

![[Evidence.base#forClaim]]

## Potentially Relevant Papers


### Contradicting Evidence

- [[@Allan_2022_impact_English#^Allan-2022-impact-En-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > EP patients presented to the ED more than LEP patients (23% vs. 14%, p < 0.001).
  > *The evidence suggests higher emergency department presentations for EP (English Proficient) patients compared to LEP (Limited English Proficiency) patients, which implies LEP patients may have less healthcare engagement. This contradicts the claim that LEP patients have lower recurrence likelihood when interpreting services are used.*
- [[@Barwise_2018_Differences_code#^Barwise-2018-Differe-L9]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Patients with LEP were more likely to have restraints used (OR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.11-1.65; P=.003).
  > *The evidence suggests increased use of restraints for patients with limited English proficiency, which implies worse clinical outcomes, contrary to the claim of lower recurrence likelihood when interpreting services are used*
- [[@Betzamel_2023_Longer_Times_1#^Betzamel-2023-Longer-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Patients who required interpreter use were 2.4 times more likely to experience extended TTTA compared to patients who did not require an interpreter (odds ratio = 2.42, 95% confidence interval = 1.84-3.18, p < .001).
  > *The evidence suggests patients requiring interpreters were 2.4 times MORE likely to experience extended treatment time, which opposes the claim of lower recurrence likelihood when interpreting services are used*
- [[@Biswas_2020_Impact_limited#^Biswas-2020-Impact-l-L10]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > LEP was an independent predictor of 30-day heart failure hospitalizations (odds ratio 2.01, 95% CI 1.21-3.36; P = 0.008).
  > *The evidence suggests LEP is associated with higher hospitalization risk (odds ratio > 1), which implies worse health outcomes, contrary to the claim that interpreting services reduce recurrences*
- [[@Biswas_2020_Impact_limited#^Biswas-2020-Impact-l-L8]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > LEP patients had higher heart failure hospitalization rates within 30 days of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (5.1% vs. 2.0%, P < 0.001).
  > *Evidence shows LEP patients had higher hospitalization rates, which suggests worse health outcomes, contrary to the claim of lower recurrence likelihood when interpreting services are used*
- [[@Bower_2023_Association_Limited#^Bower-2023-Associati-L6]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > There were no statistically significant differences in 72-hour return visits between patients with LEP and English proficiency (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.92 - 1.06).
  > *The statistical evidence shows no significant difference in return visits between limited English proficiency (LEP) and English-proficient patients, which directly challenges the claim that interpreter services reduce recurrence likelihood*
- [[@Bower_2023_Association_Limited#^Bower-2023-Associati-L7]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > There were no statistically significant differences in 7-day return visits between patients with LEP and English proficiency (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.93 - 1.05).
  > *The statistical evidence shows no significant difference in return visits between LEP and English-proficient patients, which does not support the claim that interpreter services reduce recurrences*
- [[@Calvillo-Ortiz_2022_Language_Proficiency#^Calvillo-Ortiz-2022--L6]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > LEP status was associated with higher odds of death in matched analysis (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.03-2.47).

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - LEP patients have lower medication-related self-efficacy than English-proficient patients, a modifiable adherence risk.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - LEP patients had lower medication learning self-efficacy than English-proficient patients but equal taking self-efficacy - @Zhang_2018_Medication_Related]]
- [[EVD - Only 11 percent of LEP patients reported receiving written medication information in their preferred language - @Zhang_2018_Medication_Related]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

The deficit is specific to *learning about* medications (not the act of taking them) and is compounded by very low access to written medication information in patients' languages.

> "among patients with chronic illnesses, LEP patients had lower medication-related self-efficacy scores than EP patients, which may put them at greater risk for medication taking errors and lower adherence." (Zhang, 2018)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - LEP patients use remote medication refill systems less than English-proficient patients, risking wider adherence disparities.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - LEP patients had much lower odds of using any remote medication refill system than English-proficient patients - @Moreno_2016_Disparities_Use]]
- [[EVD - The remote-refill disparity was driven by Internet refills while telephone refill use did not differ by LEP status - @Moreno_2016_Disparities_Use]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

Because remote refills are an adherence-supporting service, lower uptake among LEP patients — concentrated in the English-only Internet channel — risks widening medication-adherence disparities unless refill systems are made language-accessible.

> "Increased reliance on current systems for remote medication refills may increase disparities in health outcomes affecting LEP patients with poor access to telephone and Internet medication refills." (Moreno, 2016, p. 282)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Language-concordant automated telephone self-management is a valid scalable way to assess medication adherence in linguistically diverse populations.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Language-concordant ATSM assessed self-reported adherence as well as a structured interview when validated against pharmacy-claims CMG - @Ratanawongsa_2018_Language-concordant_automated]]
- [[EVD - Optimal adherence by claims was lower among ATSM respondents reporting more missed days for blood pressure and cholesterol but not diabetes pills - @Ratanawongsa_2018_Language-concordant_automated]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

This is a measurement claim: it concerns how validly adherence can be *assessed* via a language-concordant tool ([[ART - Language-concordant automated telephone self-management (ATSM, SMARTSteps)]]), not the effect of concordance on adherence itself. Validity was modest (significant convergent gradients for 2 of 3 medication classes).

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Limited english proficiency is not necessarily associated with worse treatment adherence.md
body:
Limited English proficiency (LEP) is not necessarily associated with worse treatment adherence; in some populations, adults with LEP show no measurable difference in adherence from English-proficient adults despite being more likely to be prescribed the relevant therapy.

## Supporting Evidence

- [[EVD - Adults with LEP were more likely to be prescribed ART than EP adults (89.7% vs 83.5%) but ART adherence did not differ - @Padilla_2021_Limited_English]]

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Patients with limited english proficiency can achieve equal or better clinical outcomes than English-proficient patients when they receive care at facilities with robust support services.md
body:
Patients with limited English proficiency (LEP) can achieve equal or better clinical outcomes than English-proficient patients when they receive care at facilities that provide robust support services (including interpreter and social services), even though LEP populations carry greater socioeconomic risk.

## Supporting Evidence

- [[EVD - Adults with LEP and diagnosed HIV were more virally suppressed than EP adults (77.5% vs 69.6%) - @Padilla_2021_Limited_English]]
- [[EVD - Adults with LEP were more likely to be prescribed ART than EP adults (89.7% vs 83.5%) but ART adherence did not differ - @Padilla_2021_Limited_English]]
- [[EVD - Adults with LEP were more likely than EP adults to receive care at RWHAP-funded facilities (79.0% vs 67.0%) - @Padilla_2021_Limited_English]]

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Patients with limited english proficiency have shorter hospital stays when interpreting services are used.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py). Migrated to grounded evidence; see also the (redundant) grounded claim [[CLM - Professional interpretation at admission and discharge shortens length of stay for LEP inpatients]] — candidate for merge.

- [[EVD - LEP inpatients without a professional interpreter on both admission and discharge had a 0.75-1.47 day longer length of stay - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]
- [[EVD - Adjusted mean length of stay was 5.06 days with no interpreter vs 2.57 days with interpreters on both admission and discharge - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]
- [[EVD - Only 39% of LEP inpatients received professional interpretation on both admission and discharge while 13.8% received none on either day - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

- [[EVD - There was no significant association between access to professional interpreter services via telephone and length of stay for LEP patients]]

## Potentially Relevant Papers


### Contradicting Evidence

- [[@Anderson_2020_Association_Primary#^Anderson-2020-Associ-L10]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Among hospitalized patients, there was no difference in length of stay between English and non-English speakers.
  > *The evidence directly states no difference in length of stay between English and non-English speakers, which opposes the claim that interpreter services reduce hospital stay length*
- [[@Barwise_2023_Comparative_costs#^Barwise-2023-Compara-L6]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > In a propensity matched cohort of survivors, patients with LEP had significantly greater mean costs for all outcomes.
  > *The evidence suggests higher costs for LEP patients, which may imply longer or more complex hospital stays, contrary to the claim of shorter stays when interpreting services are used*
- [[@Betzamel_2023_Longer_Times#^Betzamel-2023-Longer-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Patients who required interpreter use were 2.4 times more likely to experience extended total time to appointment (TTTA) (odds ratio = 2.42, 95% confidence interval = 1.84-3.18, p < .001).
  > *The evidence suggests patients with interpreter needs actually experienced longer time to appointment (TTTA), which implies potential delays or barriers, rather than supporting shorter hospital stays as claimed in the original statement*
- [[@Betzamel_2023_Longer_Times_1#^Betzamel-2023-Longer-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Patients who required interpreter use were 2.4 times more likely to experience extended TTTA compared to patients who did not require an interpreter (odds ratio = 2.42, 95% confidence interval = 1.84-3.18, p < .001).
  > *The evidence indicates patients requiring interpreters were more likely to experience extended time to treatment/admission, which suggests longer hospital stays, opposite to the claim of shorter hospital stays*
- [[@Chua_2022_Differences_End-of-Life#^Chua-2022-Difference-L7]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > LEP was independently associated with increased hospital length of stay (mean difference 4.12 days; 95% CI, 1.72-6.53; p < 0.001).
  > *The evidence indicates that LEP patients actually have LONGER hospital stays (increased length of stay by 4.12 days), which directly contradicts the claim that interpreter services reduce hospital stay length*
- [[@Clara_2025_Interpreter_Modalities#^Clara-2025-Interpret-L5]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Limited English proficiency patients had higher 72-hour unplanned revisit rates (2.8%) compared to controls (0.7%), which was statistically significant (P = .05).
  > *Higher unplanned revisit rates suggest potential complications or incomplete care, which likely indicates longer or more complex hospital stays, not shorter stays as the original claim suggests*
- [[@Clark_2022_Relationship_Between#^Clark-2022-Relations-L7]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > LEP patients experienced greater lengths of stay in healthcare settings.
  > *The evidence indicates that LEP patients actually experienced longer hospital stays, which directly opposes the claim that interpreter services reduce length of stay*
- [[@Diamond_2010_hospitals_measure#^Diamond-2010-hospita-L7]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Many hospitals informed patients of their right to receive language services only in English.
  > *The evidence suggests that hospitals are not effectively providing language services in patients' native languages, which would likely impede communication and potentially lead to longer hospital stays for patients with limited English proficiency, contrary to the claim*
- [[@Douglas_2014_Non-English_speaking#^Douglas-2014-Non-Eng-L5]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > Hospital length of stay was shorter for English speakers.
  > *The evidence indicates hospital stays were shorter for English speakers, which is opposite to the claim that interpreter services would reduce hospital stay length for patients with limited English proficiency*
- [[@Douglas_2014_Non-English_speaking#^Douglas-2014-Non-Eng-L4]] (confidence: 0.90)
  > There was no difference in ICU length of stay between English-speaking and non-English-speaking groups.
  > *The evidence specifically indicates no difference in length of stay between language groups, which directly challenges the claim that interpreter services reduce hospital stay duration*

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Professional interpretation at admission and discharge shortens length of stay for LEP inpatients.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - LEP inpatients without a professional interpreter on both admission and discharge had a 0.75-1.47 day longer length of stay - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]
- [[EVD - Adjusted mean length of stay was 5.06 days with no interpreter vs 2.57 days with interpreters on both admission and discharge - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

Within a single LEP inpatient population, receiving a professional interpreter at admission (and especially at both admission and discharge) is associated with a significantly shorter hospital stay after adjusting for age, gender, illness severity, language, and diagnosis. Interpretation at admission appears to carry the greatest effect, consistent with the patient history accounting for most of the information needed to formulate a correct diagnosis.

> "Our research shows that LEP patients who did not receive professional interpretation on date of admission and discharge experienced a more lengthy hospitalization with an average of 1.5 days longer than LEP patients who received these services. Specifically, a patient's access to professional interpretation at admission seems to have had the greatest effect on LOS." (Lindholm, 2012, p. 1298)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Professional interpretation at admission or discharge lowers 30-day readmission for LEP inpatients.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - LEP inpatients with no interpreter on admission or discharge had a higher 30-day readmission rate (24.3% vs 14.9%) - @Lindholm_2012_Professional_language]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

LEP inpatients who received professional interpretation at admission and/or discharge were less likely to be readmitted within 30 days than those who received no interpretation, after adjusting for age, gender, severity, language, and length of stay. The unadjusted gradient (24.3% readmitted with no interpreter vs 14.9% with interpreters on both days) supports the same direction.

> "The likelihood of a patient being admitted within 30 days of discharge seems to be associated with having an interpreter at either admission and/or discharge." (Lindholm, 2012, p. 1299)

node_file: Discourse Graph/Claims/CLM - Providing verbal medication information can mitigate LEP patients lower medication-related self-efficacy.md
body:
## Supporting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that support this claim (→ EVD—supports→CLM edges by sync_relations.py).

- [[EVD - Verbal medication information narrowed the LEP learning self-efficacy gap but had no effect for English-proficient patients - @Zhang_2018_Medication_Related]]
- [[EVD - LEP patients had lower medication learning self-efficacy than English-proficient patients but equal taking self-efficacy - @Zhang_2018_Medication_Related]]

## Contradicting Evidence

> [!info] EVDs that oppose this claim (→ EVD—opposes→CLM).

## Other Notes

Self-efficacy is a modifiable predictor of medication adherence; because verbal medication information specifically raises LEP (not EP) learning self-efficacy, consistently providing it is a candidate intervention to improve LEP adherence.

> "These findings suggest that consistently providing VMI to LEP patients can improve their self-efficacy in learning about medications and may be an effective intervention to improve medication adherence." (Zhang, 2018)
